routes.label: Construct three lattice points or obstruct a second one
Construct a distinct indexed integer-direction family
Construct points and restrict the slope

question:
In the following table, each question mark is to be replaced by “Possible” or “Not Possible” to indicate whether a nonvertical line with the given slope can contain the given number of lattice points (points both of whose coordinates are integers). How many of the \(12\) entries will be “Possible”?

[Figure 1](figures/2024_AMC_10B_Q19_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The useful questions are whether one lattice point forces more lattice points, and whether two lattice points restrict the slope.

A line with zero slope has equation \(y=k\). If \(k\) is an integer, it contains the three lattice points \((0,k),(1,k),(2,k)\), and indeed every point \((n,k)\) with integer \(n\). If \(k\) is not an integer, it contains no lattice points. Thus this row has “Possible” only under zero and more than two.

For a nonzero rational slope, write \(m=p/q\), where \(p,q\) are integers, \(p\ne0\), and \(q>0\). If the line contains a lattice point \((x_0,y_0)\), its equation is
\[
y-y_0=\frac pq(x-x_0).
\]
It therefore also contains \((x_0+q,y_0+p)\) and \((x_0-q,y_0-p)\). These three lattice points are distinct because their horizontal coordinates differ. Consequently, exactly one or exactly two lattice points is impossible. More than two is possible on \(y=(p/q)x\). Zero is possible on
\[
y=\frac pqx+\frac{1}{2q},
\]
because integer coordinates would require \(qy-px=1/2\), whereas the left side is an integer. This row also has two “Possible” entries.

Now let \(m\) be irrational. Two distinct lattice points on a nonvertical line have different horizontal coordinates, so their slope would be
\[
\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1},
\]
a ratio of integers with nonzero denominator. This is rational, so a line of irrational slope has at most one lattice point. The line \(y=mx\) contains exactly one, the origin. The line \(y=m(x+1/2)\) contains none: integer coordinates would imply
\[
m=\frac{y}{x+1/2},
\]
which is rational. Here the denominator cannot be zero because \(x\) is an integer. Thus the irrational-slope row has “Possible” only under zero and exactly one.

Each of the three rows has exactly two “Possible” entries, so the answer is \(2+2+2=\boxed{6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
